noteBlocks.lede: Tell someone you walked ten kilometres and they know how far you went. Tell them you ended just over seven kilometres from home, and in which direction, and they know where you are. Mechanics keeps those two kinds of measure apart, and every Unit 2 question depends on which one you are holding.
can: Tell distance from displacement, and speed from velocity, on a real journey
Define a vector and a scalar quantity in the words the mark scheme credits
Sort any list of Unit 2 measures, weight and mass included, into the right column

noteBlocks.caption: The path she walks, dashed, and the one straight step from start to finish.

noteBlocks.md: Some measures answer one question: how much. Others answer two: how much, and which way. A measure that carries a direction is a **vector**; one that is only an amount is a **scalar**. **Distance** is a scalar: it adds up the whole path, whichever way each piece went. **Displacement** is a vector: the single straight step from start to finish, with its direction.

noteBlocks.stem: A walker goes 4 km due east and then 6 km due north. How far does she walk, and what is her displacement from where she began?

steps.decision: Distance follows the path, so the two legs simply add. No direction comes with it: it is a scalar.
The straight step from start to finish is the hypotenuse of the right angle the two legs make, so Pythagoras gives its length.
A displacement is complete only with its direction, which makes it a vector. Measured from north, the side opposite the angle is the 4 km leg east.

noteBlocks.finalAnswer: Distance $10$ km; displacement $7.21$ km at $33.69^{\circ}$ east of north, a bearing of $033.69^{\circ}$

noteBlocks.title: PhET: Vector Addition
noteBlocks.attribution: Simulation by PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder, licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (https://phet.colorado.edu)
noteBlocks.task: Drag one arrow onto the grid and turn on the magnitude and angle readouts. Move the arrow without turning it: the magnitude stays and the angle stays. Turn it: the magnitude stays and the angle changes. Those two readings together are the vector.

noteBlocks.prompt: A cyclist rides 7 km due east and then 9 km due north. Which pair is right?
noteBlocks.explain: Distance follows the path, so the legs add: $7 + 9 = 16$ km. Displacement is the straight step, the hypotenuse: $\sqrt{7^2 + 9^2} = 11.40$ km, with a direction. That is steps 1 and 2 of See it. Swapping them treats the path as the straight line; 16 km twice forgets the shortcut.

twin.prompt: A walker goes 10 km due north and then 3 km due east. Which pair is right?
twin.explain: The legs add for the distance: $10 + 3 = 13$ km. The displacement is the hypotenuse, $\sqrt{10^2 + 3^2} = 10.44$ km, shorter than the path whenever the walk turns a corner.

optionNotes.why: It swaps the two: the path he walks, 10 + 3, is the distance, and the shorter straight line from start to finish is the displacement.
It adds the legs for both, but the displacement cuts the corner, so it is shorter than the path whenever the walk turns.
It swaps the two: the path she rides, 7 + 9, is the distance, and the shorter straight line from start to finish is the displacement.
It adds the legs for both, but the displacement cuts the corner, so it is shorter than the path whenever the ride turns.

noteBlocks.text: Define it, then give an example

noteBlocks.md: The mark scheme gives one mark for a general definition and one for an example. **A vector quantity has magnitude and direction. A scalar quantity has magnitude only.** Magnitude means the size; examiners accept *quantity* in its place. The example is a separate mark: written instead of the definition, it earns only itself.

noteBlocks.title: Why the direction must travel with it
noteBlocks.md: In the drawing, two pulls of 30 N give 60 N when they point the same way and nothing when they point against each other. The number 30 alone cannot tell those apart, so a force is only described in full when its direction comes with it.

noteBlocks.stem: Three students were asked for the definition of a vector quantity, with an example. How many of the 2 marks does each answer earn?

steps.working: Ana: 'A vector quantity has magnitude and direction, for example acceleration.' 2 marks
steps.decision: A general sentence that fits every vector, then one example: the two marks the scheme sets.

steps.working: Ben: 'A vector is a force moving in a direction.' No definition mark
steps.decision: It describes one kind of vector, a force, not what every vector has. Summer 2019 examiners gave no credit for definitions like this.

steps.working: Cara: 'A vector has magnitude only, for example mass.' 0 marks
steps.decision: That is the scalar definition, and mass is a scalar: both halves describe the other kind. The word only belongs to scalars.

noteBlocks.title: Scalar and Vector Quantities - What They Are, Examples, How to Represent Vectors
noteBlocks.why: A second pass over the two definitions, with the arrows drawn. The examples are physics ones, and they match the Unit 2 lists.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which sentence defines a scalar quantity?
options: A quantity with magnitude and direction
noteBlocks.explain: A definition says what every scalar has, as Ana's line did for vectors in step 1 of See it: magnitude and nothing else. Adding direction gives the vector definition, Cara's slip turned round, and naming mass gives an example, Ben's slip: one example cannot stand for every scalar. So: a quantity with magnitude only.

optionNotes.option: A quantity with magnitude and direction
optionNotes.why: That is the vector definition: a scalar has a size and nothing else.
Mass is a scalar, but one example does not say what every scalar has, so it earns no definition mark.

noteBlocks.md: Take each measure on its own and ask one question: is a direction part of the measure itself? Every force is a vector, because it pushes or pulls along a line: weight, tension, friction and the normal reaction in the drawing. So is anything that says where a body went, or how its motion is changing. An amount with no direction, like a mass or a time, is a scalar.

noteBlocks.stem: A rope drags a 6 kg box 15 m due east across a rough floor in 5 s. Sort four measures from that sentence: the 6 kg, the 15 m due east, the 5 s and the friction on the box.

steps.working: 6 kg: a mass, so a scalar
steps.decision: It is an amount of matter and points nowhere: magnitude only.

steps.working: 15 m due east: a displacement, so a vector
steps.decision: It says how far and which way the box went, so a direction is part of it. Two rows right earn the first mark.

steps.working: 5 s: a time, so a scalar
steps.decision: A duration is only an amount; a time cannot point anywhere.

steps.working: Friction: a force, so a vector
steps.decision: Every force acts along a line in one direction, and friction points against the motion. All four rows right earn the second mark.

noteBlocks.prompt: The normal reaction is the push of a surface on a body, at right angles to the surface. Which statement about it is right?
options: It is a vector, because it pushes in a direction
It is a scalar, because it is measured in newtons
It is a scalar, because it does not make the body move
noteBlocks.answer: It is a vector, because it pushes in a direction
noteBlocks.explain: Ask whether a direction is part of the measure, as each line of See it did. The normal reaction is a force pushing at right angles to the surface, so it has a size and a direction: a vector, like the friction in step 4. Newtons give only its size.

twin.prompt: A rope is 2.5 m long. Which statement about the length of the rope is right?
options: It is a scalar, because it has a size only
It is a vector, because the rope lies along a line
It is a vector, because it is measured in metres
twin.answer: It is a scalar, because it has a size only
twin.explain: Ask whether a direction is part of the measure. A length is how long the rope is, whichever way it lies: a size and no direction, so a scalar, like the time in step 3 of See it.

optionNotes.option: It is a vector, because the rope lies along a line
optionNotes.why: The rope lies one way, but its length does not: 2.5 m is the same whichever way the rope lies.

optionNotes.option: It is a vector, because it is measured in metres
optionNotes.why: Metres measure a size, and a distance in metres becomes a vector only when it also says which way.

optionNotes.option: It is a scalar, because it is measured in newtons
optionNotes.why: Newtons measure the size of a force, but a force also acts along a line in one direction, which makes it a vector.

optionNotes.option: It is a scalar, because it does not make the body move
optionNotes.why: Whether or not the body moves, the surface still pushes one way, at right angles to it, so a direction is part of the force.

noteBlocks.text: Why weight is a vector, mass a scalar

noteBlocks.alt: The same toolbox marked 12 kilograms, drawn on the Earth and on the Moon. On each, an arrow for its weight points straight down: a long arrow on the Earth and a much shorter one on the Moon, drawn to the same scale.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 262' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><text x='105' y='36' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>On the Earth</text><rect x='73' y='70' width='64' height='50' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='105' y='101' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>12 kg</text><path d='M105 120L105 200' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M105 210L100.5 200L109.5 200Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='115' y='230' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>weight</text><text x='295' y='36' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>On the Moon</text><rect x='263' y='70' width='64' height='50' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='295' y='101' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>12 kg</text><path d='M295 120L295 124.4' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M295 134.4L290.5 124.4L299.5 124.4Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='305' y='154.4' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>weight</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: The same 12 kg on the Earth and on the Moon: the mass stays, the pull changes.

noteBlocks.md: At home, *weight* often means what the scales show, which is really the mass. In mechanics they are different measures. Mass is how much matter there is, in kilograms, and it points nowhere: a scalar. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, in newtons, and it points straight down: a vector. On the paper, weight $= mg$ with $g = 10$ m/s².

noteBlocks.stem: A toolbox has a mass of 12 kg. Give its mass and its weight on the Earth, and again on the Moon, where $g$ is about $1.6$ m/s².

steps.working: Mass: $12$ kg, on the Earth and on the Moon
steps.decision: Mass is the amount of matter in the toolbox. Carrying it somewhere else does not change it, and it has no direction.

steps.working: On the Earth: $12 \times 10 = 120$ N, straight down
steps.decision: Weight is the force of gravity, mass times $g$. It has a size and a direction, so it is a vector.

steps.working: On the Moon: $12 \times 1.6 = 19.2$ N, straight down
steps.decision: The same mass, but the Moon pulls less hard, so the force is smaller. Only the weight depends on where the toolbox is.

noteBlocks.prompt: An astronaut carries a 5 kg hammer from the Earth to the Moon. Which statement is true?
options: Its mass is unchanged and its weight is smaller
Its weight is unchanged and its mass is smaller
noteBlocks.answer: Its mass is unchanged and its weight is smaller
noteBlocks.explain: Mass is the amount of matter, so the same hammer keeps the same mass. Weight is the pull of gravity, mass times $g$, and the Moon pulls less hard, so the weight is smaller: steps 1 and 3 of See it. Shrinking the mass swaps the two measures; keeping both forgets that weight depends on gravity.

twin.prompt: A 30 kg crate is brought from Mars, where gravity is weaker than on the Earth, back to the Earth. Which statement is true?
options: Its mass is unchanged and its weight is larger
Its weight is unchanged and its mass is larger
twin.answer: Its mass is unchanged and its weight is larger
twin.explain: The crate is the same crate, so its mass is the same. The Earth pulls harder than Mars, so its weight, mass times $g$, is larger.

optionNotes.option: Its weight is unchanged and its mass is larger
optionNotes.why: It swaps the two measures: the crate keeps all its matter, and it is the pull of gravity on it that grows on the Earth.
Weight is mass times g, so where gravity is stronger the weight is larger even though the mass stays the same.

optionNotes.option: Its weight is unchanged and its mass is smaller
optionNotes.why: It swaps the two measures: the hammer keeps all its matter, and it is the pull of gravity on it that shrinks.
Weight is mass times g, so where gravity is weaker the weight is smaller even though the mass stays the same.

noteBlocks.alt: An arrow for the velocity 8i minus 3j: dashed lines show 8 units across and 3 units down, and the solid arrow joins the start to the end. A note says the speed is the arrow's length.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 262' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M60 80L300 80' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' stroke-dasharray='5 5' stroke-opacity='0.8' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'/><path d='M300 80L300 170' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' stroke-dasharray='5 5' stroke-opacity='0.8' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'/><path d='M60 80L288.8 165.8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2.4' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M300 170L286.9 170.8L290.7 160.7Z' fill='currentColor'/><circle cx='60' cy='80' r='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='1'/><text x='180' y='68' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>8 across</text><text x='310' y='130' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>3 down</text><text x='164' y='155' text-anchor='end' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>velocity</text><text x='120' y='208' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>its length is the speed</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: A velocity drawn as an arrow: its direction is the way it points, and the speed is its length.

noteBlocks.md: **Speed or velocity.** The paper prints the word in bold as a hint. A speed is one number, the length of the velocity arrow; a velocity keeps its direction, often as $x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$. In Summer 2019 most candidates stopped at the velocity where the speed was asked; in Summer 2023 examiners saw magnitudes found where the vector itself was wanted.

**A list, or two definitions.** Question 1 is usually a table of four to seven measures for 2 marks, sometimes with one row done for you (Summer 2022, Summer 2025), or two definitions with an example each for 4 (Summer 2019). One wrong row costs a mark.

noteBlocks.stem: A body moves with velocity $(8\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})$ m/s. Write down its velocity, then find its speed.

steps.decision: A velocity is a vector, so the answer keeps both components: together they carry its direction.
Speed is the size of the velocity: one number, no direction. The formula sheet gives the magnitude of $x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$.

noteBlocks.prompt: A part asks for the speed of a body whose velocity is $(5\mathbf{i} - 11\mathbf{j})$ m/s. Which answer fits?
noteBlocks.explain: The word decides it, as in step 2 of See it: speed is the size of the velocity, one number. Pythagoras on the components gives $\sqrt{5^2 + (-11)^2} = 12.08$ m/s. The vector itself answers a question about the velocity, and 16 adds the components as if they pointed the same way.

twin.prompt: A part asks for the speed of a body whose velocity is $(-8\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ m/s. Which answer fits?
twin.explain: Speed is the magnitude: $\sqrt{(-8)^2 + 5^2} = 9.43$ m/s, one number with no direction. The vector answers a velocity question, and 13 adds the sizes of the components as if they pointed one way.

optionNotes.why: That is the velocity itself, direction and all, but the question asks for the speed, its size alone.
That adds the sizes of the components, but they point at right angles, so the arrow is shorter than their sum.
That is the velocity itself, direction and all, but the question asks for the speed, its size alone.
That adds the sizes of the components, but they point at right angles, so the arrow is shorter than their sum.

noteBlocks.md:
Tell distance, along the path, from displacement, the straight step with its direction.
Define a vector (magnitude and direction) and a scalar (magnitude only), then give the example.
Sort any list by asking whether a direction is part of the measure: every force is a vector.
Keep mass (kilograms, a scalar) apart from weight (newtons, straight down, a vector).
Give a speed as one number and a velocity with its direction.

steps.decision: Distance adds up the whole path, whichever way each piece went, because it has no direction attached to it.

options: Because distance measures the path travelled, with no direction attached
Because distance is always the shortest route between two points
Because distance and displacement are two words for the same measure
whyMenu.explain: The shortest route is the displacement. Distance follows the path she actually rode, so a journey that doubles back keeps adding.

steps.working: Displacement $= 5$ km on a bearing of $036.87^{\circ}$, since $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$.
steps.decision: Displacement is one straight step from the start to the finish, so it needs both a size and a direction to be stated in full.

accepted: Displacement = 5 km on a bearing of 036.87°

items.stem: From an earlier topic: which unit is a force measured in?

options.feedback: Forces are measured in newtons, written N.
Kilograms measure mass. A force is measured in newtons.
Joules measure energy. A force is measured in newtons.
That is a speed. A force is measured in newtons.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a bearing is measured from which direction, and which way round?

options.feedback: Bearings start at north and turn clockwise, written with three figures.
The turn is clockwise, the way the hands of a clock move.
East is where an angle measured from the positive x-axis starts, which is a different convention.
North is the zero of a bearing.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a right-angled triangle has shorter sides 3 and 4. How long is the hypotenuse?

options.feedback: That adds the two sides. Pythagoras squares them first.
That is the square of the hypotenuse. The last step is a square root.

items.stem: Which of these is the definition of a vector quantity?
items.skill: The definition of a vector quantity

options.text: A quantity with magnitude and direction
options.feedback: Both halves are needed, and this is the wording CCEA credits.
That is a scalar. A vector adds a direction to the size.
That is an example rather than a definition, and CCEA refuses an example offered in place of one.

items.stem: Is weight a vector or a scalar, and why?

options.text: A vector, because it is a force and it acts downwards
options.feedback: Weight is the pull of gravity on a mass, so it has a size in newtons and a direction.

options.text: A scalar, because it is just a number of newtons
options.feedback: This is the commonest error on this question. Weight is a force, and every force has a direction.

options.text: A scalar, because it is the same as mass
options.feedback: Mass and weight are different measures: kilograms against newtons, and mass has no direction while weight does.

options.text: A vector, because it is measured on a balance
options.feedback: The instrument does not decide it. Weight is a vector because it is a force with a direction.

options.text: Speed is a scalar and velocity is a vector
options.feedback: Velocity is a speed with a direction attached, so it is the vector of the pair.

options.text: Speed is a vector and velocity is a scalar
options.feedback: It is the other way round. Velocity carries the direction.
Speed answers only how fast, so it has no direction.
Velocity names a direction as well as a size, so it is a vector.

items.stem: A runner does one full lap of a 400 m track and stops where she started. What are her distance and her displacement?

options.feedback: The path is 400 m long, and the finish is the start, so there is no displacement.
Displacement is measured from start to finish in a straight line, and here those are the same point.
The two are the other way round. She really did cover 400 m of track.
Distance counts the whole path, so a lap of the track is 400 m however it ends.

findTheMistake.stem: Cathal is classifying four measures for the opening question of a Unit 2 paper. His answers:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 calls weight a scalar. Weight is the pull of gravity on a mass, so it is a force: it has a size in newtons and it acts downwards. The confusion comes from mass, which really is a scalar and is often called weight in ordinary speech.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three of the four are right, which on a two-mark table earns the first mark. Weight is the one CCEA reports most often as misclassified, so it is worth a second look every time: if a measure is a force, it is a vector.
